paragraphs: This paper presents a physical neural network containing one thousand neurons and one million connections, each represented with seven bits. The system uses asynchronous pulse-density modulation: activity is conveyed through the density of pulses. Its hardware can evolve one thousand coupled nonlinear first-order differential equations continuously and in parallel, making the network dynamics themselves the computation.

The authors assess performance with a winner-take-all network containing all one thousand neurons. Such a network makes competing units settle on a single winner. Even though each competing neuron receives inputs and network parameters of identical magnitude, one neuron wins within six milliseconds. The authors report that this corresponds to a processing rate of 360 billion connections per second.

The hardware also supports different network configurations by loading parameters from a host system. These include feedforward networks, feedback networks, and networks for filtering information across space and time. The contribution therefore combines a demonstration of fast collective dynamics with a programmable physical platform for several kinds of neural computation.
neurips-1997-a-1-000-neuron-system-with-.tldr: A programmable neural hardware system runs one thousand neurons through one million physical connections and demonstrates rapid winner-take-all dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether speakers adapt their speech movements when the sound they hear from their own voice is altered. The motivating comparison is adaptation to prism glasses, which shift visual feedback and cause people to adjust their movements. Here, the researchers ask whether changing auditory feedback produces a corresponding adjustment in speech production.

The experiment uses a device that transforms speech signals and returns them to speakers in real time. The alterations change the perceived phonetic identity of a vowel, meaning that speakers hear their production as a different vowel sound. Participants learn to change how they produce the vowel in a direction that compensates for the altered feedback.

The adjustment also carries over to different consonant contexts and to other vowels. That transfer matters because the learned response extends beyond the particular sound context used during exposure. The findings show that speech production can adapt to changes in auditory feedback and that this adaptation can influence a broader set of speech movements.
neurips-1997-adaptation-in-speech-motor-.tldr: Speakers compensate for altered auditory feedback, and the resulting speech adaptation transfers across consonant contexts and vowels.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose the spatial grid and time resolution used in reinforcement learning for a continuous control problem. Its setting is deterministic, with continuous states and time, and an objective that discounts costs over an infinite future. Computation requires discrete approximations, making the choice of resolution part of the learning problem.

The authors propose local error estimates and algorithms that refine the grid and time discretization after examining an approximate solution. Spatial refinement follows numerical methods for the Bellman equation, which characterizes optimal value. For time refinement, they introduce a criterion based on consistency estimates, assessing how the discrete solution agrees with that equation.

The central finding is that the balance between temporal and spatial resolution is crucial for both learning rate and value-function accuracy. Refinement therefore requires coordinating two choices rather than treating each independently. The approach makes numerical approximation error an explicit guide for adapting the representation used during reinforcement learning.
neurips-1997-adaptive-choice-of-grid-and.tldr: Adaptive error estimates coordinate spatial and temporal refinement to improve reinforcement learning for continuous deterministic control.

paragraphs: A Gaussian mixture represents data using several Gaussian components, but deciding how many components to include is itself a modeling problem. This paper treats that number as an unknown to estimate alongside the other parameters. It focuses on multivariate spherical Gaussian mixtures, whose individual components have the same spread in every direction.

The authors extend reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo to this setting using a hierarchical prior model. The key capability is movement between parameter spaces belonging to mixtures with different numbers of components. Because adding or removing a component changes how many parameters a model has, the sampling procedure must handle changes in dimension as part of its operation.

The result is a sample from the joint distribution of the unknown model parameters, including the component count. This connects model-size selection with parameter estimation in one probabilistic procedure. The paper demonstrates the technique on simulated data and a vowel dataset, illustrating its application to both a constructed example and observed multivariate data.
neurips-1997-an-application-of-reversibl.tldr: Reversible-jump sampling estimates both the parameters and the number of components in multivariate spherical Gaussian mixtures.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a classifier can improve learning by choosing which classes to request examples from. The task is classification into multiple categories using labeled data. The proposed nearest-neighbor algorithm acquires samples incrementally according to a querying rule, giving the learning procedure an active role in determining the composition of its training data.

That differs from passive batch learning, where the available examples reflect the classes' prior probabilities. A query-based learner can change which classes it samples instead of accepting their natural frequencies. The experiments compare these approaches and find that the size of the improvement depends on the complexity of the Bayes rule, the optimal classification rule for the underlying problem.

The authors also describe conditions under which the sampling principle could extend beyond nearest neighbors. A learning algorithm must support a model-selection criterion, and its classification error must be calculable in terms of model complexity. These requirements connect the choice of new examples to an explicit account of how complexity affects predictive performance.
neurips-1997-an-incremental-nearest-neig.tldr: An incremental nearest-neighbor learner actively chooses classes to sample, with gains that depend on the complexity of the optimal classification rule.

paragraphs: This paper explores reinforcement learning for an automated aircraft recovery system. Such a system sits above the underlying flight controls and aims to return an aircraft from an out-of-control condition to straight-and-level flight as quickly as possible. The broader objective includes physical constraints on the aircraft and physiological constraints affecting the pilot.

The reported experiments address a simplified version involving simulated recoveries around a single axis: pitch. Using experience from a medium-fidelity aircraft simulation, the learning system develops a policy for pitch-stick inputs. In unconstrained cases, it approximates a minimum-time policy for returning to straight-and-level flight while avoiding a collision with the ground.

The system also performs simulated recoveries while respecting an acceleration constraint at the pilot station. This shows that the learning approach can incorporate a restriction relevant to the person flying the aircraft. The evidence concerns initial, single-axis simulation experiments, establishing a result for that restricted recovery task within the larger aircraft-control objective.
neurips-1997-automated-aircraft-recovery.tldr: Reinforcement learning produces rapid simulated pitch recoveries while avoiding ground strikes and can respect a pilot-station acceleration constraint.

paragraphs: This paper develops an approximate learning algorithm for Boltzmann machines using a second-order expansion of Gibbs free energy in the connection weights. It combines mean-field approximation with a linear-response correction to correlations. That correction comes from the Hessian of the free energy, a description of its curvature. The resulting computational cost grows cubically with the number of neurons.

The evaluation uses a fully connected, ten-neuron Ising spin-glass learning task. The authors compare exact Boltzmann-machine learning with first-order Weiss mean-field theory and second-order TAP mean-field theory. This comparison tests whether retaining the additional second-order terms improves the approximation used during learning.

The reported method works well for paramagnetic problems, and the TAP correction substantially improves on Weiss theory for both paramagnetic and spin-glass problems. Adding diagonal weights also improves the Weiss approximation in paramagnetic cases, but not in spin-glass cases. These findings distinguish two proposed improvements: the second-order correction helps across both regimes tested, while the benefit of diagonal weights depends on the regime.
neurips-1997-boltzmann-machine-learning-.tldr: Second-order mean-field corrections improve approximate Boltzmann-machine learning, with cubic computational cost in the number of neurons.

paragraphs: This paper applies the Aggregating Algorithm, a general method for combining prediction strategies, to online linear regression with squared error. The main assumption is that the response variable is bounded. The aim is to control how much worse the algorithm performs than an appropriate best linear regression function over the prediction sequence.

For this problem, the resulting prediction procedure resembles ridge regression but differs slightly from it. The authors use general results about the Aggregating Algorithm to derive a guaranteed bound on the performance difference. This gives a theoretical measure of competitiveness: it quantifies the additional loss the procedure may incur relative to its linear comparator.

The Aggregating Algorithm achieves the optimal constant in that bound. Ordinary ridge regression can have a constant four times worse under the same kind of comparison. This is a statement about the strength of the performance guarantee, rather than a claim that every prediction is four times more accurate. The contribution shows that a small procedural difference can matter substantially for worst-case guarantees.
neurips-1997-competitive-on-line-linear-.tldr: An aggregation-based online regression method achieves an optimal bound constant that ridge regression can miss by a factor of four.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how a visual recognition system can focus on an object while coping with other objects, clutter, and partial obstruction. It builds on a Kalman-filter model previously used to explain certain responses in visual cortex. The new contribution extends that model to scenes containing multiple objects through ideas from robust statistics.

The resulting robust Kalman filter combines top-down expectations with bottom-up sensory signals. In the model, some forms of attention emerge from that interaction. Expected object information and incoming visual evidence jointly shape processing, providing a computational account of how relevant information can be emphasized while distracting or obscured information is discounted.

Experiments demonstrate segmentation and recognition of objects and image sequences under varying amounts of occlusion and clutter. The model also offers possible functional interpretations of attention-related effects observed in visual cortical neurons. Its significance is therefore twofold: it demonstrates robust visual processing and connects that behavior to a proposed explanation of certain neural effects associated with attention.
neurips-1997-correlates-of-attention-in-.tldr: A robust Kalman-filter recognition model produces attention-like behavior through interactions between visual expectations and sensory evidence.

paragraphs: This paper presents an algorithm for approximating functions with a neural network containing one hidden layer. Its nodes use piecewise-linear sigmoidal functions. The network grows one node at a time, with each new node fitted to the residual: the part of the target function that the current network has not yet explained.

The main innovation is the procedure for fitting an individual node. It searches for a good fit by solving a sequence of quadratic programming problems. This gives the node-fitting process a structured optimization approach and provides an alternative to derivative-based training methods such as backpropagation and its extensions.

The authors report finite-step convergence, a straightforward stopping criterion, and a deterministic way to seek good local minima. They also emphasize favorable scaling and numerical robustness. These properties matter because a constructive network method repeatedly solves the node-fitting problem as it grows. The stated guarantee concerns a controlled search for local solutions; the abstract characterizes the resulting minima as good, without claiming a globally optimal network.
neurips-1997-function-approximation-with.tldr: The sweeping hinge algorithm builds a network incrementally by fitting residuals through sequences of quadratic programming problems.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian framework for matching relational models organized into hierarchies. The task is to assign discrete labels that specify matches while keeping the overall correspondence consistent. Because the representations have several levels, a proposed match can have consequences both among its peers and elsewhere in the hierarchy.

The framework expresses matching through a global cost function that gathers consistency information from different levels. Its Bayesian formulation distinguishes constraints within a level from constraints between levels. This separation makes explicit two sources of evidence: whether a match agrees with neighboring assignments at the same level, and whether it agrees with relationships across the hierarchy.

Consequently, reassigning a match can be evaluated through its effects on peers, parents, and children. This matters when an assignment that appears suitable locally creates disagreement with a broader or finer representation. The contribution is a unified formulation for assessing those connected consequences, so that discrete matching decisions can be guided by consistency across the whole hierarchical model.
neurips-1997-graph-matching-with-hierarc.tldr: A Bayesian graph-matching framework evaluates discrete assignments using consistency constraints within and across hierarchical levels.

paragraphs: This paper studies how surrounding objects can help identify an ambiguous object. Measurements may be noisy enough that an object's own observed properties do not clearly determine its class. The proposed technique adds context, defined here as the identities of accompanying objects, to the information used for classification.

The authors apply the approach to white blood cell identification. The central idea is that evidence about the other objects present can help resolve uncertainty about the cell being classified. This makes classification depend on both the cell's measurements and the contextual information supplied by its companions.

Comparisons with classification that does not use context show better performance when context is included. In the reported application, the method substantially reduces false alarms, which in turn reduces costs associated with expensive clinical tests. The practical significance is that improved classification changes the number of unnecessary follow-up actions. The paper thus links a general way of handling ambiguous observations to a concrete benefit in white blood cell identification.
neurips-1997-incorporating-contextual-in.tldr: Using the identities of accompanying objects improves white blood cell classification and reduces costly false alarms.

paragraphs: This paper considers a learning setting in which the inputs requiring predictions are already available alongside labeled training examples. Credit default prediction and medical image recognition are given as motivating applications. The central question is whether those test inputs can help shape the learned solution before their outcomes are known.

The authors propose a method that incorporates test inputs into learning. These inputs supply information about the cases on which the model will be evaluated, while the labeled examples provide the known input-output relationships. The approach therefore uses the available prediction cases as part of the learning problem, making their input information relevant to the fitted solution.

The paper reports smaller test errors than a simple solution based on training alone, with particularly strong benefits for noisy problems or small training sets. Those findings identify situations where the additional input information is especially useful. The contribution is the use of an available source of information—the test cases themselves—to improve predictions when labeled training evidence is limited or noisy.
neurips-1997-incorporating-test-inputs-i.tldr: Incorporating available test inputs into learning reduces test error, especially with noisy data or small labeled training sets.

paragraphs: This paper approaches intrusion detection by learning the characteristic behavior of individual computer users. Its premise is that a user's activity leaves a recognizable behavioral signature. If activity associated with that user no longer matches the learned signature, the system can alert an administrator to a possible security breach.

The proposed system, NNID, uses a neural network trained with backpropagation to identify users from their behavior. User identification becomes the basis for detecting unusual activity: the detector looks for a mismatch between observed behavior and the expected user profile. This provides a learned alternative to constructing hand-coded detection rules or relying on online command prediction.

The authors test NNID on a system with ten users and report 96% accuracy in detecting unusual activity, alongside a 7% false alarm rate. The two figures capture useful detection and the accompanying burden of incorrect alerts. The results support learning user profiles as an intrusion-detection approach, with alerts indicating possible breaches that warrant attention rather than establishing intrusion by themselves.
neurips-1997-intrusion-detection-with-ne.tldr: A neural network learns user behavior profiles to flag unusual activity, reporting 96% detection accuracy and a 7% false alarm rate.

paragraphs: This paper proposes representing continuously varying objects with continuous attractors in a recurrent neural network. In conventional associative memory, each stored pattern corresponds to an isolated stable state. An object seen from continuously changing viewpoints instead produces a family of related patterns. A continuous attractor represents that family as a connected set of stable states.

The network learns through pattern completion: it receives corrupted examples and is trained to restore missing information. This training develops an attractor that models the manifold from which the patterns were drawn. The paper contrasts this with simply teaching a network to retain examples, which can also leave it storing unrelated, spurious stable states.

The contribution links a representation choice to a learning task. Continuous attractors capture smooth variation, while restoration teaches the network how incomplete observations relate to that structure. Statistically, this casts unsupervised learning as regression through pattern completion instead of density estimation. The demonstrated network illustrates how learning to reconstruct examples can organize recurrent dynamics around their underlying continuous family.
neurips-1997-learning-continuous-attract.tldr: Training recurrent networks to complete corrupted patterns can produce continuous attractors that represent smoothly varying families of observations.

paragraphs: This paper introduces up-propagation, an algorithm for both interpreting observations with a neural generative model and learning that model from examples. The generative model uses top-down connections to produce patterns from hidden variables. Processing sensory input requires reversing that relationship: finding hidden-variable values that account for the observed pattern.

The inversion is iterative. A negative-feedback loop uses an error signal carried through bottom-up connections to revise the model's interpretation of the input. Top-down generation and bottom-up error propagation therefore work together, with the error communicating the mismatch that the ongoing inference process needs to address.

The same error signal also trains the generative model, connecting inference and learning through a shared mechanism. The authors benchmark the algorithm against principal component analysis using images of handwritten digits. That experiment places the method alongside another approach to representing image variation. The central contribution is an explicit feedback procedure that uses a generative network both to explain incoming patterns and to learn from them.
neurips-1997-learning-generative-models-.tldr: Up-propagation uses bottom-up error feedback to infer hidden variables and train a top-down neural generative model.

paragraphs: This paper formulates nonlinear dimensionality reduction as preserving the intrinsic distances among observations. When data lie on a curved manifold, those distances follow paths along the manifold. The aim is to find a Euclidean feature-space representation whose ordinary distances reproduce these path-based, or geodesic, distances as closely as possible.

The proposed method, isomap, recovers low-dimensional nonlinear structure in perceptual datasets, including a manifold of face images. The authors report reliable recovery in settings where conventional global mapping methods become trapped in local minima. Preserving the manifold's distance structure is intended to produce features with meaning across the entire collection of observations.

The recovered representation also makes certain perceptual transformations easier to compute. Interpolation, extrapolation, and analogy can be expressed as simple linear operations in feature space even when their effects are highly nonlinear in the original observation space. The significance is therefore both descriptive and operational: the map captures underlying structure and provides coordinates in which manipulating that structure becomes simpler.
neurips-1997-mapping-a-manifold-of-perce.tldr: Isomap preserves distances along a data manifold to recover globally meaningful features that simplify nonlinear perceptual transformations.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the dynamics of networks containing excitatory and inhibitory neuron populations. It constructs a Lyapunov function, a mathematical tool for establishing whether a dynamical system approaches a stable state. The construction assumes symmetric interactions within each population and antisymmetric interactions between the excitatory and inhibitory populations.

From this function, the authors derive sufficient conditions for global asymptotic stability of fixed points. These conditions provide a guarantee that the relevant dynamics settle toward fixed activity states. If the conditions are violated, stable limit cycles may occur, allowing activity to continue in a repeating pattern. Failure of the conditions permits this possibility without making oscillation inevitable.

The paper also expresses the dynamics in minimax and dissipative Hamiltonian forms, revealing connections to optimization and classical mechanics. These formulations give complementary mathematical views of the same network behavior. Together, they help explain how the assumed interaction structure can support either convergence to fixed points or sustained cyclic activity.
neurips-1997-minimax-and-hamiltonian-dyn.tldr: A Lyapunov analysis gives stability conditions for structured excitatory-inhibitory networks and connects their dynamics to optimization and mechanics.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to learn the structure of nonlinear Markov networks with continuous variables. Such networks describe conditional independence: which variables cease to provide additional information about one another once other variables are known. This graphical representation is useful when the relationships being modeled do not have a natural causal ordering.

The authors use neural network structures to model the quantitative relationships between variables. The overall problem can be viewed as estimating a non-Gaussian, multidimensional probability distribution while exploiting conditional independencies. Learning therefore concerns both the pattern of relationships and the nonlinear numerical behavior associated with them.

The principal goal is to discover structure that provides insight into the process behind the data. Applications to two datasets show that the approach can find interesting structures, and the paper also briefly addresses inference. Its contribution is a way to combine graphical descriptions of dependence with flexible neural modeling, so that continuous-variable modeling can yield an interpretable account of how variables relate as well as a distributional representation.
neurips-1997-nonlinear-markov-networks-f.tldr: Neural models of continuous-variable relationships support learning Markov-network structures intended to reveal dependencies in the underlying process.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to learn an ordering of alternatives when the available information is incomplete. A limited number of observations may provide only partial evidence about which hypotheses deserve higher positions. The task is to turn that evidence into a useful ranking, making uncertainty in the observations central to the learning problem.

The authors describe two algorithms for ranking hypotheses and apply them under two learning criteria: probably approximately correct learning and expected loss. These criteria give different ways to judge a ranking procedure. The first concerns obtaining approximately correct results with high probability, while the second concerns the loss expected from the learner's decisions.

The paper evaluates the ranking procedures on synthetic datasets and on real data from spacecraft design optimization. The reported results demonstrate their effectiveness in those settings. Using both kinds of data connects the proposed procedures to an applied problem where alternatives must be ordered from available evidence. The contribution combines concrete ranking algorithms with evaluation under two explicit views of learning quality.
neurips-1997-on-efficient-heuristic-rank.tldr: Two hypothesis-ranking algorithms learn from incomplete information and are evaluated on synthetic data and spacecraft design optimization.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theory of online learning in nonlinear networks trained on finite datasets. It focuses on soft-committee machines, a particular class of nonlinear network. Accounting for a finite collection of training examples brings the analysis closer to learning situations in which a fixed dataset supplies the successive updates.

The authors derive dynamical equations for a set of order parameters, quantities that summarize relevant aspects of the learning process. These equations describe training through a reduced collection of variables. They become exact in either of two limiting settings: when the networks are linear or when the training set is infinite.

Preliminary comparisons with simulations suggest that the theory captures some consequences of having a finite training set. The authors also identify a specific unresolved issue: it may not correctly account for local minima. The result is therefore a partial extension of learning dynamics to a more realistic nonlinear setting, with exact limiting cases and a stated difficulty in describing where the optimization process can become trapped.
neurips-1997-on-line-learning-from-finit.tldr: A dynamical theory captures some finite-training-set effects in nonlinear online learning but may not correctly describe local minima.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a representational limitation of recurrent cascade correlation networks. The question is whether these networks can model every finite-state automaton, a system that changes among finitely many states in response to inputs. Earlier impossibility results explicitly restricted the units to sigmoid or hard-threshold transfer functions.

The new proof covers any finite, discrete transfer function used by the network's units. For each such choice, there are finite-state automata that the architecture cannot model, regardless of how many units it contains. Increasing network size therefore does not remove the demonstrated limitation within this class of transfer functions.

The proof also applies to continuous transfer functions with finitely many fixed points, including sigmoid and radial-basis functions. This widens the scope beyond the activation choices covered by earlier results. The contribution concerns what the architecture can represent, rather than whether a particular training procedure succeeds: under the stated transfer-function conditions, some finite-state computations remain unavailable even when the network is allowed additional units.
neurips-1997-rcc-cannot-compute-certain-.tldr: Recurrent cascade correlation networks cannot represent certain finite-state automata even with unlimited units across broad classes of transfer functions.

paragraphs: This paper develops reinforcement learning for control problems in which both state and time are continuous and the system evolves stochastically. Control affects the state's systematic motion, while a random component represents disturbances or fluctuations. The objective evaluates expected discounted reinforcement across the possible trajectories, including a terminal contribution when the state exits the domain.

The authors state the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation satisfied by the optimal value function. This equation connects the value of a state to the consequences of available control choices. They then use a finite-difference method to construct a convergent approximation scheme, translating the continuous mathematical problem into a form suitable for computation.

A reinforcement learning algorithm is built from that approximation scheme, and the paper proves its convergence to the optimal solution. The main contribution is this connection between continuous stochastic control, numerical approximation, and learning. The learning rule inherits a mathematically grounded route toward optimality through the equation defining value and the convergent scheme used to approximate it.
neurips-1997-reinforcement-learning-for-.tldr: A finite-difference approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation yields a reinforcement learning algorithm with a convergence proof for continuous stochastic control.

paragraphs: This paper examines a dispute about what the timing of reading aloud reveals about the reading process. Human experiments show increased naming latency for irregular words when the irregularity occurs earlier in the word. Dual-route models predict this effect, and it has been interpreted as evidence for a left-to-right component of reading.

The disputed claim is that a single-route connectionist model processing information in parallel cannot reproduce that position-dependent effect. The authors present network models that do show the interaction. Their result provides a counterexample to the claim that this particular behavioral pattern is unavailable to parallel single-route models.

The paper also uses orthographic neighborhood statistics—the patterns among words with related spellings—to explain the effect. This connects naming latency to the structure of the word relationships represented by the models. The finding matters for interpreting behavioral evidence: an effect that appears to reflect serial processing can also arise in a parallel connectionist account through the organization of spelling neighborhoods.
neurips-1997-serial-order-in-reading-alo.tldr: Parallel single-route reading networks reproduce an irregularity-position effect previously claimed to require serial processing.

paragraphs: This paper studies a modification of the Gaussian distribution in which all variables are constrained to be nonnegative. That restriction changes the kinds of energy functions the distribution can use, allowing nonconvex forms. The energy function shapes which configurations receive greater probability, so this change expands the structures that the model can represent.

The authors illustrate the distribution's expressive capacity through two multimodal examples, called competitive and cooperative distributions. Multimodality means that probability can concentrate around several distinct configurations. These examples demonstrate how the nonnegative formulation supports richer arrangements of likely states within the proposed distribution family.

The cooperative example can represent translations of a pattern, connecting the distribution to the modeling of pattern manifolds. A translated pattern belongs to a related family of configurations, and representing that family is a step toward describing continuous pattern variation. The paper's contribution is thus both a distributional construction and an illustration of its potential for representing structured families of patterns.
neurips-1997-the-rectified-gaussian-dist.tldr: Constraining Gaussian variables to be nonnegative enables nonconvex, multimodal models, including one that represents translations of a pattern.
